title: Pre-Columbian Americas
description: Explore the major civilizations of North and South America before European contact.
objectives: Describe major pre-Columbian civilizations
Explain how geography shaped these cultures
Recognize contributions to world history

lessons.title: Civilizations of the Americas
lessons.content: The Americas were home to sophisticated civilizations long before Europeans arrived.
examples: Maya: advanced writing, astronomy, mathematics; Classic period 250–900 CE; Mesoamerica
Aztec (Mexica): Tenochtitlan; powerful empire through tribute and trade; 1300–1521 CE
Inca: Tawantinsuyu; largest empire in pre-Columbian Americas; 1438–1533 CE; Andes Mountains

lessons.title: North American Cultures
lessons.content: Hundreds of distinct cultures thrived in North America.
examples: Mississippian culture: Cahokia — population 20,000+; built large earthen mounds
Ancestral Puebloans: cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde; sophisticated irrigation
Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy: democratic confederacy of six nations — influenced U.S. Constitution

title: European Exploration and Colonization
description: Study European exploration of the Americas and the establishment of colonies.
objectives: Explain motivations for exploration (3 Gs: Gold, Glory, God)
Describe major explorers and their routes
Analyze the impact of colonization on Indigenous peoples

lessons.title: Age of Exploration
lessons.content: European nations competed to explore and claim territory in the Americas.
examples: Columbus (1492): Spain → Caribbean
Hernán Cortés (1519–1521): conquered the Aztec Empire with 600 soldiers and Indigenous allies
Francisco Pizarro (1532): conquered the Inca Empire; used smallpox as an inadvertent weapon

lessons.title: Columbian Exchange and Its Consequences
lessons.content: Contact between Old and New Worlds transformed both.
examples: Devastating disease: 50–90% of Indigenous populations died from European diseases
Forced labor and enslavement of Indigenous peoples
Encomienda system: Spanish colonizers given land and Indigenous workers

title: Colonial America
description: Examine the establishment and growth of the thirteen original colonies.
objectives: Describe the three colonial regions
Compare colonial life in different regions
Explain how the colonies developed distinct identities

lessons.title: Three Colonial Regions
lessons.content: Geography shaped colonial economies, societies, and values.
examples: New England: rocky soil, short growing season → fishing, shipbuilding, small farms; Puritan influence; town meetings
Middle Colonies: fertile land, diverse settlers (Dutch, German, Quaker) → 'breadbasket' of wheat and grain
Southern Colonies: warm climate, long growing season → tobacco, rice, indigo plantations; enslaved labor; aristocratic society

lessons.title: Colonial Government
lessons.content: Colonists developed traditions of self-government that would fuel revolution.
examples: Mayflower Compact (1620): Pilgrims agreed to self-govern
House of Burgesses (1619, Virginia): first representative assembly in the Americas
By 1775, all colonies had elected assemblies

title: The American Revolution — Causes and Effects
description: Analyze the causes, events, and legacy of the American Revolution.
objectives: Trace the escalating tensions between Britain and the colonies
Analyze the Declaration of Independence as a political document
Evaluate the Revolution's impact on different groups

lessons.title: Escalating Tensions
lessons.content: A series of British policies pushed colonists toward revolution.
examples: Stamp Act (1765): tax on documents → protests, 'taxation without representation'
Townshend Acts (1767): taxes on imports → colonial boycotts
Boston Massacre (1770): British soldiers kill 5 colonists → outrage
Tea Act and Boston Tea Party (1773): colonists dump 342 chests of tea
Intolerable Acts (1774): British punishment galvanizes colonial unity

lessons.title: Impact on Different Groups
lessons.content: The Revolution meant different things to different people.
examples: Many enslaved people fought on the British side, hoping for freedom (promised by Lord Dunmore's Proclamation)
Native Americans mostly supported Britain (who had limited western settlement)
Women contributed to the war effort but did not gain legal rights
Roughly 1/3 of colonists were Loyalist and either fled or were persecuted

title: Building a New Nation
description: Examine the critical period from the Articles of Confederation through the Constitution.
objectives: Explain the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation
Describe the Constitutional Convention
Analyze the structure of the new government

lessons.title: Articles of Confederation
lessons.content: The first U.S. government was intentionally weak — and it showed.
examples: No power to tax; no national army; no power to regulate commerce
Shays' Rebellion (1786): debt-ridden farmers revolted; Congress couldn't stop it
This crisis convinced leaders a stronger government was needed

lessons.title: The Constitutional Convention
lessons.content: In 1787, delegates crafted a new framework for government.
examples: Great Compromise: bicameral Congress — House (by population) + Senate (equal per state)
3/5 Compromise: enslaved people counted as 3/5 of a person for representation (deeply immoral)
Federalism: power divided between national and state governments
Bill of Rights (1791): first 10 amendments protecting individual rights

title: Westward Expansion and Manifest Destiny
description: Analyze the ideology of Manifest Destiny and its human consequences.
objectives: Define Manifest Destiny
Trace U.S. territorial expansion
Evaluate the impact on Native Americans and Mexico

lessons.title: Manifest Destiny
lessons.content: Many Americans believed it was their God-given destiny to expand across the continent.
examples: Louisiana Purchase (1803): Jefferson doubled U.S. territory for $15 million
Mexican-American War (1846–1848): U.S. gained California, Texas, and the Southwest
Oregon Territory (1846): U.S. and Britain divided the Pacific Northwest

lessons.title: Human Costs
lessons.content: Expansion came at enormous human cost.
examples: Indian Removal Act (1830): forced relocation of tribes east of the Mississippi
Trail of Tears (1838): Cherokee Nation forced to march 1,000+ miles; ~4,000 died
Mexican citizens in acquired territories lost land and rights despite treaty promises

title: Slavery and the Road to Civil War
description: Trace the deepening sectional crisis over slavery from 1820–1860.
objectives: Explain the Missouri Compromise and Compromise of 1850
Describe the abolitionist movement
Analyze events that pushed the nation toward civil war

lessons.title: Compromises and Crises
lessons.content: A series of compromises delayed but could not prevent civil war.
examples: Missouri Compromise (1820): drew a line dividing free/slave territory
Compromise of 1850: California enters free; Fugitive Slave Act enrages northerners
Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854): 'popular sovereignty' → 'Bleeding Kansas' violence
Dred Scott decision (1857): enslaved people have no rights; unconstitutional to restrict slavery in territories

lessons.title: Abolitionist Movement
lessons.content: A growing movement demanded the immediate end of slavery.
examples: Frederick Douglass: escaped enslaved man; powerful orator and writer
Harriet Tubman: Underground Railroad conductor; freed ~70 people
Harriet Beecher Stowe: Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) turned millions against slavery
John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry (1859): terrified the South

title: Reconstruction and Its Aftermath
description: Evaluate the achievements and failures of Reconstruction, and the rise of Jim Crow.
objectives: Describe Reconstruction's goals and achievements
Explain how Reconstruction ended and why
Trace the rise of Jim Crow laws and their impact

lessons.title: Reconstruction Achievements
lessons.content: Reconstruction (1865–1877) brought important constitutional changes.
examples: 13th Amendment (1865): abolished slavery
14th Amendment (1868): equal citizenship; due process; equal protection
15th Amendment (1870): Black men's right to vote
Freedmen's Bureau: education, healthcare, legal aid for 4 million formerly enslaved people

lessons.title: End of Reconstruction and Jim Crow
lessons.content: Reconstruction was undermined by violence, politics, and white supremacy.
examples: KKK and White League: terrorized Black voters and officials
Compromise of 1877: federal troops withdrawn; Republicans give up Reconstruction for the presidency
Jim Crow laws (1877–1965): legal segregation in Southern states — 'separate but equal'
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): Supreme Court upheld segregation

title: The Industrial Age and Progressive Era
description: Explore industrialization's transformation of America and the Progressive response.
objectives: Describe the transformation of American industry 1865–1900
Identify problems of the Gilded Age
Explain Progressive reforms

lessons.title: Industrial Transformation
lessons.content: After the Civil War, the U.S. became the world's largest industrial economy.
examples: Transcontinental Railroad (1869): connected the nation; built largely by Chinese and Irish immigrants
Standard Oil (Rockefeller) and Carnegie Steel: massive monopolies
By 1900, the U.S. produced more steel than Britain and Germany combined

lessons.title: Progressive Reforms
lessons.content: Reformers used investigative journalism and legislation to address industrial abuses.
examples: Muckrakers: Upton Sinclair's 'The Jungle' exposed meatpacking conditions → Pure Food and Drug Act (1906)
Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire (1911): 146 workers died; led to fire safety and labor laws
Child labor laws: keyed to 'Progressive' movement; children under 14 banned from factories (1916 Keating-Owen Act)

title: America in the 20th Century — Overview
description: Survey major events in 20th-century American history from WWI to the Cold War.
objectives: Trace U.S. involvement in WWI and WWII
Describe the New Deal
Explain the beginning of the Cold War

lessons.title: World Wars
lessons.content: America played decisive roles in both World Wars.
examples: WWI (1917 entry): Zimmermann Telegram and unrestricted submarine warfare brought U.S. in; decisive tipping of balance
Great Depression: WWI's aftermath, Prohibition, speculation bubble → crash of 1929
WWII: Pearl Harbor → total mobilization; 16 million served; Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended the Pacific war

lessons.title: Cold War Beginnings
lessons.content: After WWII, the U.S. and USSR became competing superpowers.
examples: Truman Doctrine (1947): U.S. would resist Soviet expansion anywhere
Marshall Plan: $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe → keeps it out of Soviet orbit
NATO (1949): military alliance; Soviet atomic bomb test that year changed everything
